young.html: Franz Kafka lived in Prague and worked in an insurance office by day. At night he wrote strange stories that feel like dreams.

In The Metamorphosis, a young man named Gregor Samsa works very hard as a traveling salesman to support his parents and his sister. One morning he wakes up and finds he has turned into a giant bug! He can't talk to his family anymore. His sister brings him food at first, but as time goes on the family grows tired and afraid, and they start to forget that the bug is still Gregor. The story asks: what makes someone part of a family?

young.name: gb-kafka-family
young.cap: Pick a family member and see how they treat Gregor in each part of the story.

young.html: For parents: the story is sad and ends with Gregor's death. It is often read in high school; younger children may prefer to hear the summary and talk about the questions.

Kindness without words. Gregor couldn't speak, but he could still feel. Play a game: try to tell your family something important ("I'm hungry," "I'm sad," "thank you") without any words. How hard is it to be understood? How can we be kind to someone who can't tell us what they need?

full.html: Franz Kafka (1883–1924) was a German-speaking Jewish writer in Prague, then part of Austria-Hungary. He trained as a lawyer and worked for a workers' accident insurance institute, writing in his free hours. His relationship with his forceful father troubled him all his life. The Metamorphosis (Die Verwandlung) was written in 1912 and published in 1915, one of the few works he published. Before he died of tuberculosis he asked his friend Max Brod to burn his unpublished manuscripts; Brod refused, and published The Trial and The Castle.

About quotations: the first English translation of The Metamorphosis appeared after 1930, and the translations are still under copyright, so this lesson describes the story in our own words. See "Read the full text" above for where to find it.

Part I. Gregor wakes to find himself changed into an enormous insect. His first worry is that he has missed his train and will lose his job, which pays the family's debts. The chief clerk from his firm arrives to check on him. When Gregor finally opens the door, the clerk flees and his father drives him back into his room.

Part II. His sister Grete takes charge of feeding him and cleaning his room. Gregor learns to hide under the couch so as not to frighten her. The family discovers they have more savings than he knew, and they begin to work. When Grete and her mother clear out his furniture, Gregor clings to a picture on the wall; his mother faints, and his father, in a rage, pelts him with apples. One lodges in his back.

Part III. Wounded and neglected, Gregor grows weak. The family takes in three lodgers. One evening Grete plays the violin, and Gregor, moved by the music, creeps out. The lodgers see him and give notice. Grete tells her parents they must get rid of "it," since if it were really Gregor he would have gone away himself. That night Gregor dies. The relieved family take a tram ride into the spring countryside, making plans and noticing that Grete has grown into a young woman.

full.name: gb-kafka-family
full.cap: The family's changing treatment of Gregor: our summary.

full.html: Kafka never explains the transformation. He tells an impossible event in calm, exact, everyday prose. The horror lies less in Gregor's new body than in how quickly a family can stop seeing a person in someone who can no longer provide for them.
The word "Kafkaesque" now names situations that are absurd, nightmarish and bureaucratic, where a person is trapped by forces he cannot understand.

Looking for the one right meaning. Readers have seen illness, disability, a son's guilt toward his father, the deadening effect of work, and Kafka's own sense of being an outsider. Kafka asked that the insect never be drawn on the book's cover; the story works by staying open.

items: Ovid's Metamorphoses, an old book of transformations, usually turns people into animals as a punishment or a rescue by the gods; Kafka's change has no cause and no rescue.
Dostoevsky, in Notes from Underground, also has a man compare himself to an insect.
Freud, in this era's volumes, wrote of the power of fathers in a child's inner life, a theme Kafka also explored in his "Letter to His Father."
Beckett and the later "theater of the absurd" learned from Kafka's calm telling of the impossible.
Is a person loved for who they are, or for what they do for others?
Why does Gregor worry first about his job?
Is Grete cruel at the end, or worn out? Can she be both?
Why might telling a strange event in plain words make it more powerful?

questions: If someone in your family changed in a way no one understood, what would you do?
Grete was kind to Gregor at first. Why do you think she changed?
Gregor kept loving music even when he couldn't speak. What does that tell you about him?
Why do you think the family felt happy at the end? Should they have?
How can we remember that someone who is sick or different is still the same person inside?
care: A sad story with an injury and Gregor's death, told without graphic detail. Often read in high school.
